opus-5.5.text:
I think it can still work, but only under a fairly narrow set of conditions, and people often underestimate how narrow they are.

The first condition is that the hardware target has to be stable for longer than your model's lifecycle. If you co-design an architecture around a specific accelerator, its memory bandwidth, interconnect, and the ratio of compute to memory, you're making a bet. If the next generation of chips changes those ratios, which happens every year or two now, a lot of that refinement becomes a liability. So it works when you control the hardware or have strong visibility into the roadmap, not when you're chasing whatever is in the market this quarter.

The second condition is that the use case has to be clearly defined and high volume. If you know you're serving, say, long-context agentic workloads, or very short latency-sensitive chat, or on-device inference with a tight memory budget, then the shape of inference is predictable. You know roughly the prefill-to-decode ratio, the batch sizes, the KV cache pressure. Then decisions like how many active parameters in an MoE, how you compress attention, how you lay out experts across devices, really pay off, because you're optimizing a cost curve you'll run billions of times.

The third condition, which matters most to me, is that the optimization can't come at the expense of the model's general capability ceiling. Many hardware-friendly tricks look great on throughput benchmarks but quietly hurt reasoning or long-range dependency handling, and you only find out after post-training or RL. So the refinement has to be validated end to end, not just at the kernel level. The good cases are where the efficiency gain and the capability are aligned, for example, a cheaper attention mechanism that also lets you train on much longer contexts, so you actually get a better model, not just a cheaper one.

When those three line up, a stable hardware target, a well-understood workload, and no capability tax, co-design is very powerful, and frankly it's one of the few places smaller teams can beat bigger ones on cost. When they don't, I think the safer approach is a relatively clean, general architecture, and pushing efficiency into the inference system and the engineering layer, where it's easier to adapt as things change.

r001.rationale: The response says architecture refinements should be validated end to end, including after post-training or RL, but does not say that a team’s understanding of post-training informs its architecture judgments during pretraining.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it can still work, but only under a fairly specific condition: when you genuinely own the whole stack, or at least have very tight control over it. If the same team decides the model architecture, knows exactly which chips it will run on, and understands the real use cases on the product side, then co-designing the model around the hardware makes a lot of sense. You can shape the attention mechanism, the expert routing, the KV cache layout, the precision choices, all around what that particular hardware does well and what the workload actually looks like. You get real efficiency gains that a general-purpose model simply leaves on the table.

But the moment any one of those three things is out of your hands, the approach gets fragile. If the hardware roadmap is decided by someone else, your carefully tuned architecture can become suboptimal within a generation or two. If the use cases are not clear, you end up over-fitting the design to a guess about demand. And if the model team and the infra team are separate organizations with different incentives, the coordination cost eats most of the benefit.

There's also a second condition, which is that the architecture has to still be "general enough" in the dimensions that matter for capability. You can specialize a lot of the systems-level details, memory bandwidth, sparsity patterns, how you batch inference, without touching the fundamental scaling properties. Where I think people get into trouble is when they let hardware constraints bend the parts of the design that actually determine how well the model learns. Then you have a very fast model that is not as smart as it should be, and users notice that immediately.

So my short answer would be: it works when you are vertically integrated enough to control the variables, when you have a clear, stable sense of the inference workload, and when you are disciplined about which parts of the architecture you specialize and which you leave alone. Under those conditions, I actually think it is one of the biggest remaining levers, because the cost of serving these models is now a first-order problem, not an afterthought.

r001.rationale: The response says success depends on control of the model, hardware, and use cases, but does not identify post-training understanding informing architecture judgments during pretraining.

astra-6.text: I think it can still work when the constraints are clear and relatively stable—when you know which hardware the model will run on, what workloads it will handle, and what latency and memory limits you need to meet. Then you can design the architecture around those constraints and measure whether it delivers a real advantage. But if the hardware or use cases keep changing, that specialization can quickly become a limitation. The efficiency gains have to justify both the design effort and the flexibility you give up.

r001.rationale: The response says specialization can work when hardware, workloads, and limits are clear and stable. It does not identify a team’s post-training understanding informing architecture judgments during pretraining.
